text:
Alice M.: Heads-up — saw a weird spike in on-demand GPU spend last night tied to a Karpenter provisioner burst. 
Ben K.: ugh, details? which cluster/region?
Alice M.: prod-gpu (us-west-2). We had ~6 extra p4d nodes spin up over 20m then lingered for ~45m. Cost shock on the dashboard.
Carlos R.: any events in cloudprovider or ENI limits? sometimes ENI failures cascade and nodes stall in Pending.
Alice M.: I checked: no ENI exhaustion on account level, but a few AZs had IP pressure. Karpenter logs show repeated attempts: 
```
I0325 02:11:04.123 ProvisionerController reconcile provisioner/prod-gpu - scheduling for instanceType p4d
I0325 02:11:12.456 LaunchTemplate error: network interface limit reached for availability zone us-west-2b
I0325 02:20:33.789 Node became ready but no pods scheduled (taints?)
```
Ben K.: hmm. Did the provisioner have consolidation enabled? and what was TTL?
Alice M.: consolidation is on, but TTLSecondsUntilExpired was 3600 (1h) — so they stayed a while before being reclaimed. Also we had burstCapacity: 10 which was probably overly permissive for the weekday traffic.
Dana S.: For context, prod-gpu has some long-running batch jobs that can tolerate delays, but transient starvation triggers burst. We should tune both burst and TTL.
Carlos R.: Suggestion: lower burstCapacity to 3 for weekdays, 6 for peak windows; reduce TTL to 300s (5m) for nodes with zero pods; and enable zoneAntiAffinity to avoid overloading a single AZ ENI pool.
Alice M.: I sketched a quick patch to the provisioner that we can try in staging: 
```
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1alpha5
kind: Provisioner
metadata:
  name: prod-gpu
spec:
  consolidation:
    enabled: true
  ttlSecondsUntilExpired: 300
  limits:
    resources:
      cpu: "2000"
      nvidia.com/gpu: "12"
  provider:
    subnetSelector:
      kubernetes.io/cluster/prod: "true"
    securityGroupSelector: {}
  requirements:
    - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      operator: In
      values: [us-west-2a,us-west-2b,us-west-2c]
  providerSpecific:
    burstCapacity: 3
```
Ben K.: providerSpecific isn't a real field; use `limits` + `startupTaints` + `consolidation` + a separate annotation for burst. Also ensure instanceTypes includes a mix so we don't strictly request p4d and blow budget.
Dana S.: We should also add a watchdog that reconciles nodes stuck in NotReady/Unschedulable after X minutes and force-terminate to avoid lingering billing. Could be a simple controller or a scheduled job that watches node conditions and uses AWS API to terminate.
Carlos R.: Agree. Add metrics/tracing to capture the lifecycle so we can correlate provisioner decisions with ENI failures + pod pending time.
Alice M.: Action list: 1) push a staging provisioner with TTL=300 and burst=3 (Ben/Dana) 2) add AZ anti-affinity and diversify instanceTypes (Carlos) 3) implement short watchdog (Dana) 4) add dashboard alert for >3 GPU nodes launched in 15m outside expected autoscale windows (Alice).
Ben K.: I'll prep the staging manifest and validate in staging cluster tomorrow morning.
Dana S.: I'll prototype the watchdog as a cronjob for now, then we can harden to controller if useful.
Carlos R.: I'll add some Grafana panels + tracing hooks to the provisioning pipeline and wire an alert.
Alice M.: If this goes well, we can roll to prod with a canary provisioner targeting a small namespace first. Also thinking about a rate limiter on the provisioner to cap node creation rps.
Ben K.: Rate limiter makes sense. Karpenter has `concurrency` knobs in the controller flags; we can adjust.
karpenter-bot: note: Provisioner prod-gpu had 8 launches in last 24h, median startup 12m, 95th pct 47m.
Alice M.: Thanks bot. Ok team — let's sync in the 10:30 standup to coordinate the staging change. I'll drop the manifests in the infra repo under `infra/karpenter/provisioners/prod-gpu-staging.yaml`. :thumbsup:
